title: Delta Lake Internals
subtitle: How SQL commands become files + transaction-log commits
mantra: Every Delta write = read a snapshot, write new files (or deletion vectors), validate optimistically, and commit one atomic log version.
objectives: You can replay a Delta log in your head and say which files form any snapshot.
You can explain how UPDATE/DELETE become file rewrites or deletion vectors.
You can use DESCRIBE HISTORY, time travel and RESTORE to investigate and repair bad data.
You can explain why time travel is not a backup and how VACUUM retention affects it.
You can write correct MERGE statements (SQL + Python), including NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, and deduplicate CDC sources.
You can explain optimistic concurrency, isolation levels and row-level concurrency.
You can debug MERGE failures, concurrency exceptions, 'storage didn't shrink' and 'time travel broke'.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Delta Table
sections.hook: A Delta table is not 'a folder of Parquet files' — it is whatever the transaction log says it is.

blocks.text: Zoom in on the bottom of the Databricks stack. Today we open the **Delta table** box and look at files and commits.

blocks.caption: The stack from the previous chapter — we now open 'Delta tables'

blocks.text: Goal: when you see a `MERGE`, an `UPDATE`, a concurrency error or a `VACUUM`, you can **predict** what happens to the data files and to `_delta_log`. Not just recite 'Delta = Parquet + log'.

**Delta Lake** is the default table format in Databricks. It extends Parquet data files with a **versioned transaction log**, which gives ACID semantics, metadata management, batch/streaming interoperability and table versioning.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE dev_training.sales.orders (
  order_id    BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  amount      DECIMAL(10,2),
  status      STRING
)
USING DELTA;
blocks.caption: A plain e-shop orders table

blocks.text:
orders/
├── part-00000-....parquet      <- columnar data
├── part-00001-....parquet
├── part-00002-....parquet
└── _delta_log/                 <- versioned table state
    ├── 00000000000000000000.json   (version 0)
    ├── 00000000000000000001.json   (version 1)
    ├── 00000000000000000002.json   (version 2)
    └── ...
blocks.caption: What the storage layer conceptually holds

items.def: The **data files**: real rows, stored column by column (Parquet).
Folder holding the **versioned state** of the table: one JSON commit file per version.
A JSON file named with a **20-digit zero-padded** version number, e.g. `00000000000000000003.json`.
Each normal commit creates a new **atomic** version with a monotonically increasing number: 0, 1, 2, 3…
One entry inside a commit (e.g. `add`, `remove`). A commit = an atomic set of actions that turns the previous snapshot into the next.

blocks.text: Example: `CREATE TABLE` was version 0. Now you insert two orders:

part-A.parquet
order_id | customer_id | amount | status
---------+-------------+--------+-------
       1 |         101 |  20.00 | NEW
       2 |         102 |  30.00 | NEW

_delta_log/00000000000000000001.json
  version 1:  ADD part-A.parquet
blocks.caption: One INSERT -> one new data file + one commit
Very simplified add action (real JSON is richer)

blocks.text: A real `add` action can also carry **partition values**, **modification time** and **file-level statistics** (record count, min/max per column). Those stats power data skipping (Chapter 6).

blocks.title: The first big idea
blocks.text:
The table is **the set of logical files that the transaction log says belong to the current snapshot** — not every `.parquet` file sitting in the folder.
`physical storage ≠ logical current table state`

blocks.label: Think first: storage has A.parquet, B.parquet, C.parquet but the current snapshot lists only A and C. Is B part of the table?
blocks.text: **No.** B may be an old file still needed for time travel, or one waiting to be cleaned up by `VACUUM`. A `SELECT` on the current version never reads it.

Parquet files
+ optional deletion vectors
+ _delta_log versions (JSON commits)
+ checkpoints
---------------------------------
= Delta table state
blocks.caption: Storage-side formula to make instinctive

blocks.title: "Parquet already stores data, so why do I need Delta?"
blocks.text: Parquet defines a **columnar file format**, but it does not define **transactional table state across many files**. Delta adds a versioned transaction log, atomic commits, snapshot isolation, schema enforcement/evolution, DML (`MERGE`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`), concurrency control, history/time travel and physical optimization features over those files.

sections.title: Snapshots, ADD/REMOVE & Checkpoints
sections.hook: A snapshot is just the result of replaying the log — once you can replay it in your head, Delta stops being magic.

blocks.text: A **snapshot** is the table as of one version. You get it by **replaying** the log actions from the start (or from a checkpoint).

blocks.caption: Replay the log to compute each snapshot

blocks.text: So `SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 2` must read exactly **{B, C, D}** — the files of that snapshot, not whatever is current today.

blocks.title: MVCC
blocks.text: Delta uses **MVCC (multi-version concurrency control)**: every reader picks one consistent snapshot through the transaction log and reads only its files.

items.title: ADD file
points: This logical file now **participates** in the snapshot.
Written by INSERT, UPDATE, MERGE, OPTIMIZE…

items.title: REMOVE file
points: This file **no longer participates** in the current snapshot.
Is **NOT** `rm file` — the bytes stay on storage.
Kept as a **tombstone** for a while.

blocks.text: Why keep removed files around? So that **older snapshots** and **concurrent readers** that started earlier keep working. Physical deletion happens later, typically via **VACUUM**.

items: Snapshot isolation for readers that started before the change
Recovery / history semantics — until retention expires and cleanup runs

blocks.title: Library catalogue
blocks.text: The data files are books on the shelves; the log is the **catalogue**. 'REMOVE' crosses a book out of the catalogue — the book stays on the shelf until the cleaner (VACUUM) comes.
**Problem:** a table with 1,000,000 commits. If every reader replayed v0 → v1 → … → v1,000,000, query planning would be painfully slow.

v0.json  v1.json ... v100.checkpoint  v101.json  v102.json  v103.json
                          │              │          │          │
snapshot v103 = load checkpoint v100 + replay 101 + 102 + 103
(NOT replay 0 → 103)
blocks.caption: Checkpoints summarize the log up to a version

blocks.text: A **checkpoint** stores a summary of table state up to some version in **Parquet-based** structures. **Checkpoint V2** is designed for better scalability and concurrency on large / frequently updated tables.

blocks.title: Don't rely on checkpoint frequency
blocks.text: The exact checkpoint interval is an **implementation/performance detail** that Databricks may adjust. Application code must never assume 'a checkpoint every exactly N commits'.

blocks.title: Never hand-edit `_delta_log`
blocks.text: Do not edit `00000000000000000152.json` or delete transaction files to 'fix' a table. The log **is** the transactional protocol. Use supported commands: `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE`, `RESTORE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `VACUUM`, `OPTIMIZE` and the supported APIs.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a file exists but a query doesn't read it
questions: Is this file referenced by the current snapshot, or only by older versions?
Was it removed by an UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE/OPTIMIZE commit (tombstone)?
Is it just waiting for VACUUM after the retention window?

sections.title: UPDATE & DELETE: Copy-on-Write
sections.hook: Object storage has no 'database pages' — so how can a row change? By swapping files atomically.

blocks.text: Delta supports SQL DML. Logically an `UPDATE` means:

blocks.label: Before you read on: why can't Delta just open the Parquet file and change the bytes of row 2?
blocks.text: Parquet files are **immutable**, compressed, columnar blobs on object storage. Changing one value in place is not supported — and readers using the old snapshot still need the old file.
The classic Delta mechanism is **copy-on-write**: write a new file containing the changed row plus the untouched rows, then swap files in one commit.

A.parquet (old)          B.parquet (new)
1 | 20 | NEW             1 | 20 | NEW
2 | 30 | NEW      ==>    2 | 30 | SHIPPED
3 | 40 | NEW             3 | 40 | NEW

commit:  REMOVE A  +  ADD B
before: snapshot -> A      after: snapshot -> B
blocks.caption: UPDATE via file rewrite (the first mental model)

blocks.text: A more realistic **conditional update** from the e-shop: late shipments get a 5% discount.

blocks.code:
UPDATE ecommerce.silver.orders
SET
  status = 'LATE',
  amount = amount * 0.95
WHERE status = 'SHIPPING'
  AND order_ts < current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS;

blocks.text: **DELETE** is just as simple. With a predicate, or without one — which logically deletes **all rows** (the table itself stays).
`DELETE` on Delta supports fairly complex predicates and subqueries (with some limitations).

before            after
1 NEW             1 NEW
2 CANCELLED  ==>  3 SHIPPED
3 SHIPPED
blocks.caption: State changes atomically

blocks.title: Atomic = no half states
blocks.text: No reader may ever see 'half old + half new'. A reader sees the whole old snapshot or the whole new one.

blocks.title: Logical removal ≠ physical removal
blocks.text: After `DELETE`, the old files can stay on storage (history/time travel) until `VACUUM` runs.

blocks.title: Why UPDATE/DELETE matter in a lakehouse
blocks.text: On plain Parquet folders, mutation semantics are hard. With Delta, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `MERGE` are **transactional** operations — that's why we say Delta gives **database-like table semantics on object storage**.

sections.title: Deletion Vectors
sections.hook: Rewriting a 1 GB file to delete one row is absurd — deletion vectors fix that.

blocks.text: Picture a huge Parquet file: **1 GB, 2,000,000 rows**. You want to delete **1 row**. The naïve copy-on-write model does:

blocks.caption: Very expensive for one row

blocks.text: Databricks has **deletion vectors (DV)**: instead of immediately rewriting the file, Delta records *which rows* are logically deleted.

A.parquet  +  DV: "row 72832 is logically deleted"

read A  ->  apply deletion vector  ->  don't return row 72832
blocks.caption: Merge-on-read: the file stays, a small marker hides rows

blocks.text: DVs can speed up **DELETE, UPDATE and MERGE**. For an `UPDATE`, the old row version is marked deleted in the DV and the new row version is written to a small **supplemental data file**.

items.title: With DV
points: + metadata marks the row as deleted
cheap write; reads apply the DV

blocks.text: So we correct our mental model. 'UPDATE one row → always rewrite the whole file' is **no longer generally true**:

logical table change
        │
Delta chooses an implementation
        ├── file rewrite (copy-on-write)
        └── deletion vector + supplemental data
(depends on table features / runtime / engine)
DVs must be **enabled on the table**. Databricks recommends them unless you have a compatibility constraint with older clients.

blocks.title: Table features upgrade the protocol
blocks.text: Enabling table features (like DVs) can **upgrade the Delta protocol** and make the table incompatible with older Delta clients/readers.

blocks.label: Think first: a 3 GB Parquet file, you delete 2 rows. Why is a DV much cheaper than an immediate rewrite?
blocks.text: The engine just records that those 2 rows are logically deleted. It does **not** rewrite the other millions of rows of the 3 GB file right now.
Physically purging DV-soft-deleted data needs two steps: rewrite the affected files, then clean up the old ones after retention.

blocks.caption: Physical purge of soft-deleted rows

blocks.title: DVs also help concurrency
blocks.text: Because a row change doesn't always need a full file rewrite, two writers touching **different rows of the same file** can avoid conflicts (row-level concurrency, section 11).

sections.title: DESCRIBE HISTORY & Time Travel
sections.hook: 'The data broke around noon' — history + time travel turn that panic into a 3-query investigation.

blocks.text: **DESCRIBE HISTORY** is your first Delta debugging tool. It lists table versions in **reverse chronological order** with operation metadata.

blocks.code: DESCRIBE HISTORY dev_training.sales.orders;

head: version
timestamp
operation
blocks.caption: Conceptual output (newest first)

items.def: WRITE, MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE, RESTORE, OPTIMIZE…
e.g. the MERGE predicate, write mode.

blocks.text: History retention (the log) is **30 days by default** (`delta.logRetentionDuration`).

blocks.title: Don't start by guessing
blocks.text: Someone says 'data broke around 12'. Run `DESCRIBE HISTORY` and look for: **which operation** changed the table, **who**, **when**, **what metrics** it had.
**Time travel** reads an older snapshot. It never changes the current table.

blocks.code:
old_df = (
    spark.read
         .option("versionAsOf", 121)
         .table("ecommerce.silver.orders")
)
# by time instead: .option("timestampAsOf", "2026-09-26 10:00:00")
# path-based equivalents exist where appropriate
blocks.caption: Time travel from PySpark

blocks.text: Real debugging workflow — 'today `customer_id` became null':

blocks.code:
SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders VERSION AS OF 124;  -- looks right
SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders VERSION AS OF 125;  -- broken!
DESCRIBE HISTORY prod.silver.orders;  -- which operation made v125?

items: Find the operation that created the bad version
blocks.caption: History-driven debugging

blocks.title: Ask yourself when 'someone broke the data'
questions: When was the data last known to be correct?
Which version(s) were committed between 'good' and 'bad' in DESCRIBE HISTORY?
What operation, by which user/job, created the first bad version — and what do its operationMetrics say?
If I time-travel to the previous version, is the data correct there?
Do I fix forward, or RESTORE to the last good version?

sections.title: RESTORE & Why Time Travel Is Not a Backup
sections.hook: RESTORE rolls the table forward to an old state — and history has an expiry date.

items.title: RESTORE
points: `RESTORE TABLE … TO VERSION AS OF n`

blocks.text:
v124  good
v125  bad
v126  RESTORE  (state equivalent to v124)
blocks.caption: RESTORE does not delete history — it appends

blocks.title: History stays history
blocks.text: Restoring v124 while current is v125 does **not** delete v125. A new transaction (v126) is committed whose state equals v124. Restore to v7 from v10 → you get **v11**.

blocks.label: Think first: why is it GOOD that RESTORE appends a version instead of deleting the bad ones?
blocks.text: You keep a full audit trail (who restored, when) and you can still inspect — or even return to — the 'bad' versions while investigating.
Now the classic exam/interview trap: **time travel is not a backup**. Databricks says explicitly not to use table history as a long-term backup strategy.

head: Retention
Default
Controls
blocks.caption: Two different clocks

blocks.text: To time travel to version N you need **both** the log entries of N **and** the data files of N. VACUUM can delete the files even while the history entry is still visible.

history metadata exists
         ≠
all old data files still exist

blocks.title: Trap: 'Delta history = backup'
blocks.text: False. Retention and VACUUM limit history/time travel. For real backups use a proper backup/replication strategy (e.g. deep copies to another location).

sections.title: VACUUM: Physical Garbage Collection
sections.hook: DELETE makes rows disappear from queries; VACUUM makes bytes disappear from storage.

blocks.caption: Why old files pile up

blocks.text: A and B may still be needed for older snapshots. After the retention interval, **VACUUM** removes files that are no longer referenced by any version inside the retention window.

blocks.code:
VACUUM dev_training.sales.orders;                  -- default 7 days
VACUUM dev_training.sales.orders RETAIN 168 HOURS; -- 168 h = 7 days

blocks.title: Never `VACUUM … RETAIN 0 HOURS` blindly
blocks.text: Deleting old/uncommitted files too early can break **time travel**, **long-running readers**, **long-running writers** (whose not-yet-committed files look 'unreferenced') and **recovery**. Databricks recommends at least 7 days and has a safety check (`spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled`) that blocks dangerously short retention.

blocks.title: Red flag answer
blocks.text: "I want to save storage, so `VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS` every hour." → always wrong in an exam.
**Production bug: DELETE worked, storage didn't shrink.** A 10 TB table; you delete everything before 2020. Queries no longer return those rows, yet storage stays near 10 TB.

blocks.code: DELETE FROM orders WHERE event_date < DATE'2020-01-01';

items: Logical delete ≠ immediate physical file deletion.
Old files are kept for snapshots/time travel.
With DVs, the **original file may still be the current physical input**, with the deleted rows merely masked.
Physical purge: `REORG TABLE … APPLY (PURGE)`, then `VACUUM` once the retention has passed.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when storage didn't shrink after DELETE
questions: Is this actually a bug, or just logical vs physical deletion?
Are deletion vectors enabled, so rows are only masked inside still-current files?
Has VACUUM run since the delete — and has the retention window passed?
Do I need REORG TABLE … APPLY (PURGE) before VACUUM?

blocks.text: **Production bug: time travel stopped working.** Yesterday `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 80` worked; today it fails.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when an old version is no longer queryable
questions: What does DESCRIBE HISTORY show — did a VACUUM run?
With which retention?
Do the data files of v80 still exist, or only its history entry?

blocks.title: History entry ≠ queryable version
blocks.text: VACUUM can remove physical files required by older versions, so a visible history entry doesn't guarantee that version is still readable.

sections.title: MERGE Fundamentals
sections.hook: MERGE is the most important Delta command for a data engineer: one atomic statement for insert + update + delete.

blocks.text: Target `prod.silver.customers` holds Maria/Athens, John/Patras, Anna/Volos. A source batch arrives: John moved to Athens, George (id 4) is new.

head: id
name
city
→ action
blocks.caption: UPDATE + INSERT = upsert

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.customers AS target
USING staging.customer_updates AS source
ON target.id = source.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET
    target.name = source.name,
    target.city = source.city
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (id, name, city)
  VALUES (source.id, source.name, source.city);
blocks.caption: Basic upsert

items.def: The real table I want to change.
When a source row and a target row are considered **the same entity**.

blocks.text:
source row
                  │
   does target contain a matching key?
        ┌─────────┴─────────┐
       YES                  NO
        │                   │
  WHEN MATCHED        WHEN NOT MATCHED
(UPDATE / DELETE)        (INSERT)

target row with NO matching source row
                  │
      WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
          (UPDATE / DELETE)
blocks.caption: MERGE as a Venn diagram: 3 cases

blocks.text: **WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE**: the target row exists but the source doesn't have it. Target {1,2,3,4}, source {1,2,4} → row 3. Allowed actions: **UPDATE or DELETE** (never INSERT — there's no source row to insert).

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;
blocks.caption: Full sync against an authoritative snapshot

blocks.title: NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE + incremental source = disaster
blocks.text: If the source is only **'today's changed records'** (not a full authoritative snapshot), `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` deletes almost the **entire** target. Know the **semantics of your source**, not just the syntax.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when rows vanished after a MERGE
questions: Does the MERGE contain WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE?
Is the source a full authoritative snapshot, or only today's changes?
What do the MERGE's operationMetrics in DESCRIBE HISTORY say about deleted rows?
Which version is the last good one to RESTORE?

blocks.text: `UPDATE SET *` / `INSERT *` are handy when source and target schemas are compatible:

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

blocks.text: In production you often prefer **explicit mapping**, so you know exactly which columns change (and can add audit columns):

blocks.code:
UPDATE SET
  t.name       = s.name,
  t.city       = s.city,
  t.updated_at = current_timestamp()

blocks.title: Why MERGE matters for CDC
blocks.text: A change feed usually contains inserts, updates and deletes for existing entities. `MERGE` applies all of them to the target **atomically** in one transaction — a Delta-only DML for insert/update/delete based on matching conditions.

sections.title: MERGE in Practice: Duplicates, Dedup, Python
sections.hook: The #1 MERGE failure in production is a duplicated key in the source — learn to spot and fix it in seconds.

blocks.text: Hands-on first. Build this and run it — then look at `DESCRIBE HISTORY` and you'll see a **MERGE** version.

blocks.caption: Result: 1 Maria Athens · 2 John Athens · 3 Anna Volos · 4 George Larisa

blocks.text: **The duplicate-match problem.** Target has id=7. The source has id=7/Athens **and** id=7/Volos. Which city should win?

source: id=7 city=Athens seq=10
        id=7 city=Volos  seq=11      target: id=7
MERGE ... ON target.id = source.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE
-> Athens? Volos?  ambiguous -> FAIL

There is no single answer, so the MERGE fails with a **multiple source rows matched** error (`DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE`). Databricks requires you to **preprocess the source** so no ambiguous matches exist.

blocks.title: Runtime detail
blocks.text: From **DBR 16.0+**, duplicate-match detection considers the `ON` condition **and** the relevant `WHEN MATCHED` conditions. **15.4 LTS and below** used only the `ON` condition.
Fix: keep only the **latest** change per key with a window function (CDC + window functions + MERGE in one real pattern).

blocks.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY id
           ORDER BY seq DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM staging.customer_changes
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;   -- then MERGE using this
blocks.caption: SQL dedup: latest event per key

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("sequence_number").desc())

latest = (
    source_df
      .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
      .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
      .drop("rn")
)
blocks.caption: PySpark dedup
Debug sequence for a failing MERGE

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*)
FROM ecommerce.staging.orders_updates
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
blocks.caption: Find the duplicated keys

blocks.title: Ask yourself when MERGE says 'multiple source rows matched'
questions: Is the target key really unique?
Does my source contain duplicate keys?
Which source row is the latest for each key?
Do I have a deterministic ordering field (event_sequence / updated_at / version)?
Did I deduplicate before the MERGE?

blocks.text: Typical ordering fields: `event_sequence`, `updated_at`, `version`.
**MERGE in Python** — the classic Delta API (same matching model as SQL):

blocks.code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "prod.silver.customers")
source = spark.table("staging.customer_updates")

(
    target.alias("t")
      .merge(source.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
      .whenMatchedUpdate(set={"name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
      .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
          "id": "s.id", "name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
      .execute()
)

blocks.text: Modern PySpark/Databricks also offers a DataFrame `mergeInto()` API — but master SQL `MERGE` and `DeltaTable` first: they're everywhere in existing production code.

blocks.title: No `UPDATE … FROM … JOIN`
blocks.text: Coming from PostgreSQL/SQL Server you may write `UPDATE target SET … FROM source WHERE …`. **Databricks SQL does not support this pattern.** To update from another relation, use `MERGE INTO`.

sections.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
sections.hook: Two jobs, one table, no locks — and yet no corruption. Here's the trick.

blocks.text: Jobs A and B start together on a table at **v50**. A wants to update customer 10, B wants to update customer 20. Both read snapshot v50.
Delta does **not** necessarily take a pessimistic lock ('lock the entire table, everyone wait'). It uses **optimistic concurrency control**:

items: VALIDATE: did a conflicting commit happen?
COMMIT: new atomic version, or fail/retry

blocks.text: **Why 'optimistic'?** The system assumes most concurrent transactions probably won't conflict. It lets A and B both work, and only at commit time asks: *can both results coexist consistently?* Yes → commit. No → conflict.

blocks.title: Google Docs vs a library book
blocks.text: Pessimistic = only one person can borrow the book. Optimistic = everyone edits their copy; at 'save' time the system checks whether edits collide.
**Atomic version creation**: current = v50. A commits first → **v51**. B (based on v50) must now check: *what changed from v50 → v51, and does it affect rows/files I read or change?*

v50 ──► A commits ──► v51
 │
 └─ B (read v50) validates v50→v51
        ├─ no conflict ──► commits v52
        └─ conflict    ──► transaction FAILS
                           (table not corrupted)
Put together, every Delta write follows the same skeleton:

CURRENT SNAPSHOT
             │
       READ / ANALYZE
             │
prepare data-file changes (files / DVs)
             │
   optimistic validation
      ┌──────┴──────┐
  conflict?        safe?
      │              │
    FAIL       ATOMIC COMMIT
                     │
                NEW VERSION
                     │
                NEW SNAPSHOT

sections.title: Isolation Levels & Row-Level Concurrency
sections.hook: Which conflicts are real and which are just 'same file, different row'?

blocks.text: Delta on Databricks supports two **isolation levels** for writes:

head: Level
Meaning
rows: Writes are serializable; weaker than Serializable but allows more concurrency.
Strongest: the outcome of concurrent reads **and** writes must be explainable by a fully serial order.

blocks.text: **Reads** use **snapshot isolation** — every reader sees one consistent version.

blocks.code:
ALTER TABLE my_table
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.isolationLevel' = 'Serializable');

blocks.text:
readers         -> consistent snapshots
writers         -> optimistic validation
default writes  -> WriteSerializable
blocks.caption: Memorize this trio (not the full conflict matrix)

blocks.text: **Row-level concurrency.** Older behaviour: A updates row 1 in file X, B updates row 9000 in the same file X → they could **conflict** because both touched file X.
With **row-level concurrency + deletion vectors**, Databricks detects conflicts at **row** granularity, so A and B can both succeed even though their rows share a physical file.

items: Unpartitioned tables — liquid-clustered tables also use this architecture

blocks.title: Same row still conflicts
blocks.text: Job A: `UPDATE customers SET status='A' WHERE id=10`; Job B: `… status='B' WHERE id=10`. That's a **real logical conflict**: one commits, the other fails or is serialized safely — never random corruption.

items.title: Different rows, same file
points: Now: can coexist with DVs + row-level concurrency

items.title: Same row
points: One commit wins, the other fails/retries

sections.title: Concurrency Errors & Debugging
sections.hook: A concurrency exception means Delta protected you — your job is to find out from whom.

head: Error
What it usually means
rows: A concurrent transaction wrote new data after your transaction read the table.
Another operation added files to the data/partition your operation read.
Another operation deleted/rewrote a file your operation read.
A concurrent operation changed table metadata (e.g. `ALTER TABLE`, schema-evolving write).
The table protocol changed concurrently (e.g. table feature upgrade, concurrent create/replace).

blocks.caption: Concurrency errors you will meet

blocks.title: Not corruption
blocks.text: These errors do **not** mean 'the Delta table is corrupted'. They usually mean **the optimistic concurrency system prevented an unsafe commit**. Databricks suggests **retry logic** for legitimate transient conflicts — after **re-reading fresh state**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a MERGE fails with DELTA_CONCURRENT_WRITE
questions: What other writer touched this table at the same time (DESCRIBE HISTORY)?
What rows/files/partitions did both operations read?
Are my predicates too broad?
Can I narrow the MERGE condition (e.g. add a date bound)?
Is a schema ALTER happening concurrently?
Are deletion vectors / row-level concurrency available on this table?
Should the application retry after re-reading fresh state?

blocks.text: `MERGE … ON t.id = s.id` on a huge table can have a **broad read scope**. If it is semantically correct, add a physical/time bound:

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.orders t
USING daily_updates s
ON t.id = s.id
   AND t.event_date = DATE'2026-09-16'
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
blocks.caption: Narrower ON = smaller scan AND smaller conflict domain

blocks.title: Only if semantically correct
blocks.text: Adding `t.event_date = …` is valid only if matching target rows really live on that date. Otherwise you'd insert duplicates for rows from other dates.

blocks.title: Schema changes are metadata changes
blocks.text: An `ALTER TABLE` at 12:00 while a pipeline writes can fail that writer with `MetadataChangedException` — expected semantics, not a bug. Full story in Chapter 6.
**What's next:** Unity Catalog in depth — `catalog.schema.object`, managed vs external tables, volumes, external locations, grants, and real `PERMISSION_DENIED` debugging.

pitfalls.title: Physical files ≠ table
pitfalls.text: Counting/reading .parquet files in the folder includes removed files.
pitfalls.fix: Trust the snapshot in `_delta_log`; query through the table.

pitfalls.title: REMOVE is not rm
pitfalls.text: A remove action only drops the file from the snapshot.
pitfalls.fix: Expect files to remain until VACUUM after retention.

pitfalls.title: Relying on checkpoint frequency
pitfalls.text: Checkpoint interval is an implementation detail.

pitfalls.title: Hand-editing _delta_log
pitfalls.text: Editing/deleting commit JSONs breaks the protocol.
pitfalls.fix: Use RESTORE, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, ALTER, VACUUM, OPTIMIZE.

pitfalls.title: 'UPDATE always rewrites the whole file'
pitfalls.fix: Delta chooses rewrite or DV + supplemental data.

pitfalls.title: Table features break old clients
pitfalls.text: Enabling DVs etc. can upgrade the protocol.

pitfalls.title: Time travel ≠ backup
pitfalls.text: 7-day file retention and 30-day log retention limit history.

pitfalls.title: RESTORE deletes history?
pitfalls.text: No — it appends a new version.
pitfalls.fix: Expect vN+1 equal to the restored state.

pitfalls.title: VACUUM ≠ OPTIMIZE
pitfalls.text: VACUUM deletes old unreferenced files; it doesn't compact.
pitfalls.fix: Use OPTIMIZE for layout, VACUUM for cleanup.

pitfalls.title: VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS
pitfalls.text: Breaks time travel, long-running readers/writers, recovery.
pitfalls.fix: Keep ≥ 7 days and the safety check enabled.

pitfalls.title: Storage didn't shrink after DELETE
pitfalls.text: Logical delete ≠ physical deletion (DVs mask rows).

pitfalls.title: NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE on incremental source
pitfalls.text: Deletes everything not in today's batch.

pitfalls.title: Duplicate keys in MERGE source
pitfalls.fix: Dedup with ROW_NUMBER by ordering field.

pitfalls.title: 'Run it again until it works'
pitfalls.fix: Investigate writers/scope; retry only after fresh read.

pitfalls.title: Concurrency error = corruption?
pitfalls.text: No — it's protection against an unsafe commit.

exercises.q: A Delta table consists of every `.parquet` file that physically exists in the table's folder.
exercises.explain: The table is the set of **logical** files that the transaction log references in the current snapshot. Old files (removed by UPDATE/DELETE/OPTIMIZE) can still sit in the folder for time travel or until VACUUM — they are not part of the current table.

exercises.q: A Delta table folder physically holds **50** Parquet files. The current snapshot in `_delta_log` references **37** of them. How many files are logically part of the current table?
exercises.explain: **37.** Physical existence does not imply current logical membership. The other 13 are typically tombstoned files kept for older snapshots/time travel or waiting for VACUUM.

exercises.q: Which filename is a valid Delta commit file for **version 3**?
why: Commits are JSON; Parquet is used for data files and checkpoints.
exercises.explain: Commit files use **20-digit zero-padded** version numbers with a `.json` extension. Zero padding keeps lexical order = version order when listing the folder.

exercises.q: Storage contains `A.parquet`, `B.parquet`, `C.parquet`; the current snapshot lists only A and C. What is the **most likely** reason B still exists?
options: B is corrupted and Delta skips it
B is an old file kept for time travel / not yet removed by VACUUM
B is a staging file Spark forgot to delete, so the table is broken
why: Delta doesn't skip files because of corruption; it reads exactly what the snapshot lists.
Checkpoints live inside `_delta_log`, not as data files.
Unreferenced files are expected; the table is fine.
exercises.explain: B was probably removed logically by an earlier commit (REMOVE action) and is retained for older snapshots until VACUUM cleans it up after the retention window. This is normal, not corruption.

exercises.q: Which information can a real `add` action in the transaction log carry? (choose all)
options: The full row data of the file
exercises.explain: An `add` action describes a file: path, size, `dataChange`, partition values, modification time and per-file statistics. The rows themselves live only in the Parquet file — the log stores metadata, not data.

exercises.q: Where does each thing live?
exercises.explain: Parquet files hold the **data**; `_delta_log` holds the **versioned state**: commit JSONs with actions, plus checkpoints. Checkpoints are Parquet-based but they live in the log folder and summarize metadata, not business rows.

exercises.q: Complete the storage-side formula of a Delta table.
exercises.text: Parquet files + optional [[deletion vectors|DVs|deletion vector]] + _delta_log [[versions|commits]] + [[checkpoints|checkpoint]] = Delta table state
exercises.explain: The table state is assembled from the data files, any deletion vectors that mask rows, the versioned commits and the checkpoints that summarize them. If you can rebuild this in your head, MERGE/VACUUM/concurrency become predictable.

exercises.q: Interview: **"Parquet already stores data, so why do I need Delta?"** Answer in 3–4 sentences.
exercises.model: Parquet defines how columnar data is stored in individual files, but it doesn't define transactional table state across many files. Delta adds a versioned transaction log on top of those files, giving atomic (ACID) commits and snapshot isolation. That enables DML such as MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE, schema enforcement and evolution, concurrency control, history and time travel, plus physical optimization features like OPTIMIZE, data skipping and clustering.
rubric: Parquet = file format, not table state across files
Schema enforcement/evolution, time travel, concurrency control, optimization
exercises.explain: Strong answers contrast **file format** vs **table semantics**. Mentioning only 'Delta is faster' misses the point: the core value is the transaction log and everything it enables.

exercises.q: Replay this log. Which files form the snapshot of **version 2**?
exercises.code:
v0: ADD A, ADD B
v1: REMOVE A, ADD C
v2: ADD D
why: Includes A, which was removed in v1.
A was removed; B was not.
exercises.explain: v0 → {A, B}; v1 removes A and adds C → {B, C}; v2 adds D → {B, C, D}. A is still on storage but not in the snapshot.

exercises.q: A `remove` action in the Delta log means the file is immediately deleted from cloud storage (`rm`).
exercises.explain: `remove` only means the file **no longer participates** in the snapshot. It is kept as a tombstone so older snapshots and concurrent readers still work; physical deletion happens later via VACUUM.

exercises.q: Order the steps a reader uses to build the snapshot of **v103** when a checkpoint exists at v100.
exercises.explain: Readers start from the latest checkpoint at or before the target version and replay only the JSON commits after it. Replaying from v0 would make planning expensive on tables with thousands of commits.

exercises.q: Why does Delta keep old (removed) data files around for a while? (choose all)
options: Snapshot isolation for readers that started earlier
exercises.explain: Old files serve older snapshots: in-flight readers, time travel and recovery. They do **not** speed up current queries — current queries never read them.

exercises.q: What does a Delta **checkpoint** do?
options: Stores a summarized table state so readers don't replay the log from version 0
why: Delta uses optimistic concurrency, no table lock.
exercises.explain: A checkpoint summarizes the log up to a version in Parquet-based structures. Deleting files is VACUUM; compaction is OPTIMIZE; Delta doesn't lock the table for writes.

exercises.q: Your application can safely assume Delta writes a checkpoint every exactly N commits.
exercises.explain: Checkpoint frequency is an implementation/performance detail and Databricks may adjust it (Checkpoint V2 even changes the structure). Code that depends on a fixed interval is fragile.

exercises.q: A runbook to 'undo' a bad commit. Which line is the dangerous one?
lines: SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders VERSION AS OF 151;
exercises.fix: RESTORE TABLE prod.silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF 151;
exercises.explain: Never edit or delete files in `_delta_log` — the log is the transactional protocol and hand edits can corrupt the table for every reader/writer. Use the supported `RESTORE` operation, which appends a new version equivalent to v151.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a supported way to change a Delta table's state?
exercises.explain: UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, RESTORE, ALTER TABLE, VACUUM, OPTIMIZE and supported APIs are the legit tools. Hand-editing the log bypasses the protocol.

exercises.q: A Delta `UPDATE` opens the existing Parquet file and edits the changed bytes in place.
exercises.explain: Parquet files are immutable. Delta writes new data (rewritten file or supplemental file + DV) and commits the swap atomically. Old snapshots still point at the untouched old file.

exercises.q: File A holds 3 rows; you update row 2 using classic copy-on-write. Which commit is written?
options: `REMOVE A` + `ADD B` (B = all 3 rows, row 2 changed)
why: There's no in-place row action in the log.
Old row 2 would still be visible in A → duplicate.
exercises.explain: Copy-on-write rewrites the file: B contains rows 1 and 3 unchanged plus the new row 2, and the commit atomically removes A and adds B. Adding only row 2 would leave the old row 2 visible in A.

exercises.q: Write the conditional update: orders in status `SHIPPING` older than 7 days become `LATE` and get a 5% discount on `amount`. Table: `ecommerce.silver.orders` (cols `status`, `amount`, `order_ts`).
exercises.solution:
UPDATE ecommerce.silver.orders
SET status = 'LATE',
    amount = amount * 0.95
WHERE status = 'SHIPPING'
  AND order_ts < current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS;
exercises.explain: One `UPDATE` can set several columns. The time predicate uses `current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS`. Delta then decides the physical implementation (rewrite or DV) and commits a new version.

exercises.q: Delete all cancelled orders from `dev_training.sales.orders`.
exercises.explain: `DELETE FROM … WHERE …` removes rows logically and commits a new version. The files may remain physically until VACUUM.

exercises.q: `DELETE FROM dev_training.sales.orders;` (no WHERE) drops the table object.
exercises.explain: Without WHERE it logically deletes **all rows**, but the table object, schema and history remain. Dropping the object is `DROP TABLE`.

exercises.q: A long `SELECT` is running while a `DELETE` commits on the same Delta table. What can the reader see?
options: A mix: some deleted rows, some not
Either the full old snapshot or the full new snapshot — never half
An error, because the table is locked
exercises.explain: Commits are atomic and readers use snapshot isolation: a reader is pinned to one version for its whole query. 'Half old + half new' is exactly what Delta guarantees never happens.

exercises.q: Fill in the UPDATE.
exercises.explain: Standard SQL DML. On Delta it results in a new table version; the old version stays readable via time travel.

exercises.q: Why do we say Delta gives 'database-like table semantics on object storage'? Use UPDATE/DELETE as your example.
exercises.model: On a plain Parquet folder you can't safely change a row: you'd have to rewrite files by hand and readers could see half-written states. Delta turns UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE into transactional operations: it writes new files (or deletion vectors) and atomically commits a new version in the log, so readers always see a consistent snapshot. That's the kind of mutation guarantee you'd expect from a database, on top of cheap object storage.
exercises.explain: The key is **transactional mutation**. Answers that just list commands miss why they're safe: the atomic commit to the log.

exercises.q: A 3 GB Parquet file; you delete 2 rows. Why can a deletion vector be much cheaper than an immediate file rewrite?
options: Delta records that 2 rows are logically deleted without rewriting the millions of remaining rows now
DVs delete the rows from cloud storage directly
DVs skip writing to the transaction log
why: Nothing is physically deleted — rows are masked.
Every change is still a log commit.
exercises.explain: A DV is a small marker of deleted row positions. The expensive rewrite of the 3 GB file is avoided (or deferred, e.g. to OPTIMIZE/REORG). The commit still goes through the log.

exercises.q: Order what a reader does on a table whose file has a deletion vector.
items: Read the snapshot from the log
exercises.explain: The reader combines the underlying data file with the DV state and never returns logically deleted rows. That's why reads pay a small cost while writes become cheap.

exercises.q: With deletion vectors, an `UPDATE` can mark the old row version as deleted and write the new row version into a small supplemental data file.
exercises.explain: That's exactly how DVs accelerate UPDATE (and MERGE): mark old row in the DV, write only the new row version, instead of rewriting the full file.

exercises.q: Enable deletion vectors on `dev_training.sales.orders`.
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE dev_training.sales.orders
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = true);
exercises.explain: DVs are a table feature set via a table property. Databricks recommends them unless older clients must still read the table.

exercises.q: What is the main risk when enabling a table feature such as deletion vectors?
options: It can upgrade the Delta protocol, making the table unreadable by older Delta clients
It turns the table into a Parquet table
exercises.explain: Table features may raise the minimum reader/writer protocol versions. Old engines/clients that don't support the feature can no longer read/write the table — check compatibility first.

exercises.q: In modern Databricks, updating one row **always** rewrites the whole Parquet file.
exercises.explain: That was the first mental model, but with deletion vectors Delta can choose between file rewrite and DV + supplemental data, depending on table features/runtime/engine.

exercises.q: Physically purge rows soft-deleted via deletion vectors.
exercises.explain: REORG … APPLY (PURGE) rewrites files so soft-deleted rows are physically gone from current files; VACUUM later removes the old files once they're beyond retention. Either step alone isn't enough.

exercises.q: Match each DV situation to what happens.
pairs: Row marked deleted in a DV; file kept
Reading a file with a DV
File + DV combined; masked rows skipped
Old row masked + new row in supplemental file
exercises.explain: DVs make writes cheap by deferring rewrites; reads apply the DV; PURGE finally materializes the deletion physically.

exercises.q: Read two old snapshots.
exercises.text:
SELECT * FROM dev_training.sales.orders [[VERSION AS OF]] 5;
SELECT * FROM dev_training.sales.orders [[TIMESTAMP AS OF]] '2026-09-15 10:00:00';
exercises.explain: Time travel by version number or by timestamp. Neither changes the current table.

exercises.q: What does `DESCRIBE HISTORY t` return?
options: Table versions in reverse chronological order with timestamp, user, operation, parameters and metrics
Only the last 10 queries run on the table
why: File-level info isn't listed; DESCRIBE DETAIL gives counts.
It lists writes (commits), not SELECT queries.
exercises.explain: History is versioned provenance per write: version, timestamp, user, operation, operationParameters, operationMetrics… newest first. Schema → DESCRIBE TABLE; files/size → DESCRIBE DETAIL.

exercises.q: PySpark: load `ecommerce.silver.orders` as it was at version 121 into `old_df`.
exercises.explain: The reader option `versionAsOf` (or `timestampAsOf`) selects the snapshot. It's the DataFrame equivalent of `VERSION AS OF`.

exercises.q: `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 5` makes version 5 the current version of the table.
exercises.explain: Time travel is read-only: it reads an older snapshot. Making an old state current again is `RESTORE`, which creates a new version.

exercises.q: What is the default transaction-log history retention?
why: History is finite — that's why it isn't a backup.
exercises.explain: Log history defaults to **30 days** (`delta.logRetentionDuration`). Don't confuse with the **7-day** deleted-file retention used by VACUUM.

exercises.q: A stakeholder: "Today `customer_id` in `prod.silver.orders` became NULL for many rows."

exercises.q: A pipeline corrupted data and it showed up in v101. Order your actions.
items: Time-travel and compare v100 vs v101
Identify the operation/job that created v101
Decide: fix forward or RESTORE to v100
exercises.explain: This is the test answer for 'corrupted pipeline at v101': history, compare, locate operation, then repair. Restoring first without understanding risks repeating the bug on the next run.

exercises.q: Which line has invalid time-travel syntax?
exercises.explain: The syntax is `table_name VERSION AS OF n` (or `TIMESTAMP AS OF '…'`), placed right after the table name. `AS OF VERSION` is not valid Databricks SQL.

exercises.q: Current version is **v10**. You run `RESTORE TABLE t TO VERSION AS OF 7`. What version number does the table have afterwards?
exercises.explain: RESTORE is a new transaction appended to history: v11 with state equivalent to v7. Versions 8–10 are not deleted.

exercises.q: Restoring to v7 while current is v10 deletes versions 8–10 from the history.
exercises.explain: History stays history. RESTORE commits a new version (v11) whose state equals v7; you can still inspect v8–v10 (as long as retention allows).

exercises.q: Time travel or RESTORE?

items.text: Shows up as an operation in DESCRIBE HISTORY

exercises.explain: Time travel = read only. RESTORE = a write that makes an old state current, committed as a new version and visible in history.

exercises.q: Restore `prod.silver.orders` to how it was at `2026-09-15 10:00:00`.
exercises.solution:
RESTORE TABLE prod.silver.orders
TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-09-15 10:00:00';
exercises.explain: RESTORE accepts `TO VERSION AS OF n` or `TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '…'`. It fails if the files for that version were vacuumed.

exercises.q: Delta table history is a long-term backup system.
exercises.explain: No. Default 7-day deleted-file retention (VACUUM) and 30-day log retention limit time travel. Databricks explicitly says not to use history as a long-term backup strategy.

exercises.q: To successfully time travel to version N, what must still exist?
options: Only the history entry for N
Only the data files for N
Both the log history for N and the data files of N
why: Without the log you don't know which files form N.
A checkpoint summarizes state but not the old data files.
exercises.explain: You need the log (to know which files form N) **and** the files themselves. VACUUM may delete files while the history entry is still listed — the classic 'history exists but query fails' case.

exercises.q: Match each retention fact.
pairs: Time travel to a vacuumed version
exercises.explain: Two different clocks: 7 days for data files, 30 days for log history. 168 h = 7 × 24.

exercises.q: `VACUUM t RETAIN 168 HOURS` keeps how many **days** of removed files?
exercises.explain: 168 / 24 = 7 days — exactly the Databricks default and recommended minimum.

exercises.q: VACUUM speeds up queries by compacting small files into bigger ones.
exercises.explain: VACUUM = garbage collection of old unreferenced files. Compaction/layout is OPTIMIZE. Confusing them is a very common exam trap.

exercises.q: A colleague proposes: "To save storage, run `VACUUM t RETAIN 0 HOURS` every hour." What can break? (choose all)
options: Long-running writers whose uncommitted files look unreferenced
exercises.explain: Zero retention deletes files that older snapshots, in-flight queries and in-flight writers still need. Databricks recommends ≥7 days and has a safety check that blocks short retention. Schema enforcement is unrelated.

exercises.q: Log: v0 → {A,B}, v1 → {B,C}, v2 → {C,D}. After the retention window passes, which files can VACUUM eventually remove?
options: None — VACUUM never deletes data files
exercises.explain: Current snapshot is {C, D}. A and B are referenced only by older versions; once those versions fall outside retention, VACUUM can delete them.

exercises.q: A 10 TB `orders` table. You ran `DELETE FROM orders WHERE event_date < DATE'2020-01-01'`. Queries no longer return those rows, but storage is still ~10 TB.

options.text: Recognize logical delete ≠ physical deletion; this is not necessarily a bug
options.fb: Correct: old files are kept for snapshots/time travel.

options.text: Open a P1: Delta failed to delete
options.fb: The DELETE worked logically — check the physical side first.

options.text: Re-run the DELETE until storage drops
options.fb: Re-running deletes nothing new and adds versions.

steps.prompt: DVs are enabled on the table. What does that imply?

options.text: Original files may still be current physical inputs, with deleted rows only masked
options.fb: Right: soft-deleted rows sit inside still-referenced files.

options.text: DVs physically delete rows immediately
options.fb: DVs mask rows; they don't purge.

options.text: DVs mean VACUUM alone will free the space
options.fb: VACUUM only removes unreferenced files; masked rows are inside referenced files.

steps.prompt: How do you actually free the space?

options.text: REORG TABLE orders APPLY (PURGE), then VACUUM after retention
options.fb: PURGE rewrites files without masked rows; VACUUM later deletes the old ones.

options.text: VACUUM orders RETAIN 0 HOURS
options.fb: Dangerous and still doesn't purge DV-masked rows.

options.text: OPTIMIZE orders and stop
options.fb: Rewritten files help, but old files stay until VACUUM.

exercises.explain: Two layers: logical state (DELETE) vs physical garbage collection (REORG PURGE + VACUUM). Not a contradiction.

exercises.q: Yesterday `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 80` worked. Today it fails.

options.text: DESCRIBE HISTORY orders — did a VACUUM run?
options.fb: Yes: history reveals maintenance operations and their timing.

options.text: Increase cluster size
options.fb: Not a compute problem.

options.text: Re-create the table from scratch
options.fb: Destroys evidence and history.

steps.prompt: History shows `VACUUM` ran last night. What next?

options.text: Check its retention and whether v80's data files still exist
options.fb: A history entry for v80 doesn't guarantee its files survived.

options.text: Assume the log is corrupted and delete it
options.fb: Never touch the log by hand.

options.text: Run RESTORE TO VERSION AS OF 80
options.fb: RESTORE needs the same files — it would fail too.

exercises.explain: VACUUM can remove the physical files older versions need. History entries alone don't make a version queryable — another reason time travel isn't a backup.

exercises.q: Order the steps to physically get rid of rows soft-deleted with deletion vectors.
items: DELETE FROM … WHERE … (rows masked by DV)
Wait until the retention period has passed
exercises.explain: DELETE is logical; PURGE rewrites files so the rows are physically gone from current files; after retention, VACUUM deletes the old files from storage.

exercises.q: A nightly 'storage saver' job. Which lines are dangerous?
exercises.fix:
spark.sql('VACUUM prod.silver.orders')  # default 7 days
# or RETAIN 168 HOURS; keep the safety check enabled
exercises.explain: Line 1 disables the safety check that exists precisely to block short retention, and line 2 deletes every unreferenced file immediately — breaking time travel, long-running readers/writers and recovery. Keep ≥7 days.

exercises.q: Default retention values.
exercises.text: VACUUM keeps deleted data files for [[7]] days by default, while transaction-log history is kept for [[30]] days.
exercises.explain: Two different clocks. You need both the log entry and the files to time travel, so the effective window is usually the 7-day file retention.

exercises.q: In `MERGE`, what does **WHEN MATCHED** mean?
options: A target row has no source row
A source row found a target row that satisfies the ON condition
The source and target schemas match
The row was already merged earlier
exercises.explain: WHEN MATCHED = source row ↔ target row pair via ON. Typically UPDATE (or DELETE). 'Target row with no source row' is NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE.

exercises.q: Match each MERGE clause to its meaning.
pairs: When source and target rows are the same entity
Source row has a matching target row
Source row has no target row (usually INSERT)
Target row has no source row (UPDATE/DELETE)
exercises.explain: Three cases of the Venn diagram plus the ON condition that defines 'same entity'.

exercises.q: Write an upsert: target `prod.silver.customers` (id, name, city), source `staging.customer_updates`. Update name/city on match, insert otherwise. Use explicit columns.
exercises.solution:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.customers AS t
USING staging.customer_updates AS s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.city = s.city
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (id, name, city) VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.city);
exercises.explain: Read it like a compiler: TARGET, SOURCE, ON (entity identity), then the action per case. This is the canonical upsert.

exercises.q: `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN INSERT *` is valid MERGE syntax.
exercises.explain: NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE supports only **UPDATE or DELETE** — there is no source row whose values could be inserted.

exercises.q: Your source contains only **today's changed records**. You add `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE`. What happens?
options: Only today's deleted records are removed
Every target row not in today's batch is deleted — possibly almost the entire table
Nothing; the clause is ignored for incremental sources
The MERGE fails with a syntax error
why: Delta can't know which rows are 'deleted today' — absence = delete.
Delta doesn't know your source semantics.
exercises.explain: The clause treats the source as **authoritative**: anything missing from it is deleted. Use it only when the source is a complete snapshot.

exercises.q: Complete a full sync against an authoritative snapshot.
exercises.text:
MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET [[*]]
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN [[INSERT]] *
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY [[SOURCE]] THEN [[DELETE]];
exercises.explain: `UPDATE SET *` and `INSERT *` map columns by name when schemas are compatible; NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE … DELETE removes target rows absent from the snapshot.

exercises.q: Why might production code prefer explicit `UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, …` over `UPDATE SET *`?
options: Explicit mapping shows exactly which columns change and lets you add audit columns like `updated_at`
exercises.explain: Explicit mapping is about control and readability: you know precisely what's touched, and you can add `t.updated_at = current_timestamp()`. `SET *` works when schemas are compatible.

exercises.q: Why is MERGE especially important for CDC (change data capture)?
exercises.model: A change feed typically contains inserts, updates and deletes for entities that already exist in the target. MERGE matches each change to the target by key and applies insert/update/delete in one atomic transaction, so the target stays a consistent mirror of the source state. Without it you'd need several separate statements with intermediate inconsistent states.
rubric: CDC = inserts + updates + deletes for existing entities
Applies all actions atomically in one commit
exercises.explain: The answer combines **mixed change types** and **atomicity**.

exercises.q: Target ids {1,2,3,4}; source ids {1,2,5}. Which MERGE case does each id fall into?
exercises.explain: In both → MATCHED; only in source → NOT MATCHED (insert); only in target → NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (update/delete).

exercises.q: Target ids {1,2,3,4}; source ids {1,2,4,5}. You run MERGE with WHEN MATCHED UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT, WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE. How many rows does the target have afterwards?
exercises.explain: 1,2,4 matched → updated; 5 inserted; 3 deleted (not in source). Result {1,2,4,5} = 4 rows — the target now mirrors the source exactly.

exercises.q: The source has **two rows with the same business key** that both match the same target row in an UPDATE. What do you do?
options: Nothing; Delta picks the last one
Deduplicate/rank the source first so the choice is deterministic
why: Delta does not pick silently — it errors.
There's no such switch; ambiguity must be resolved.
exercises.explain: Multiple matches make the intended final value ambiguous, so MERGE fails. Rank by a deterministic ordering field (sequence/updated_at/version) and keep one row per key.

exercises.q: Keep only the latest CDC event per key.
exercises.explain: PARTITION BY the business key, ORDER BY the sequence descending, keep rn = 1 → one latest row per key. RANK() could keep ties; ROW_NUMBER() guarantees one.

exercises.q: PySpark: from `source_df`, keep only the latest row per `customer_id` by `sequence_number`, result in `latest` (drop helper column).
exercises.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("sequence_number").desc())
latest = (source_df
          .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
          .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
          .drop("rn"))
exercises.explain: Same pattern as SQL: a window per key ordered newest first, row_number, keep 1. This is a real data-engineering pattern, not a toy window exercise.

exercises.q: MERGE on `customer_id` fails. Order the debug sequence.
items: Which source row is the latest?
Is there an event sequence / updated_at?
exercises.explain: Check uniqueness on both sides, then find a deterministic ordering field, dedup, and only then merge. Skipping the ordering-field question leads to arbitrary picks.

exercises.q: On DBR 16.0+, MERGE duplicate-match detection considers both the ON condition and relevant WHEN MATCHED conditions, while 15.4 LTS and below used only ON.
exercises.explain: Correct runtime detail: newer runtimes can avoid false 'multiple matches' errors when WHEN MATCHED conditions make only one source row applicable.

exercises.q: A PostgreSQL developer wrote this for Databricks SQL. Which line is the problem?
exercises.fix:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.customers c
USING staging.customer_updates u
ON c.id = u.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET c.city = u.city;
exercises.explain: Databricks SQL does not support the `UPDATE … FROM …` (join-update) pattern. To update from another relation, use `MERGE INTO … WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`.

exercises.q: Python: upsert `staging.customer_updates` into `prod.silver.customers` on `id` using the `DeltaTable` API (update name, city; insert id, name, city).
exercises.solution:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "prod.silver.customers")
source = spark.table("staging.customer_updates")

(target.alias("t")
   .merge(source.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
   .whenMatchedUpdate(set={"name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
   .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={"id": "s.id", "name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
   .execute())
exercises.explain: The DeltaTable builder mirrors SQL MERGE: alias target/source, merge condition, clause builders, then `.execute()` — forgetting `execute()` means nothing runs.

exercises.q: Nightly MERGE into `ecommerce.silver.orders` fails: *multiple source rows matched target row*.

options.text: GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on the staging table
options.fb: Finds which keys are duplicated in the source.

options.text: DESCRIBE DETAIL on the target
options.fb: File counts won't reveal duplicate keys.

options.text: VACUUM the target
options.fb: Irrelevant and risky.

steps.code:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*)
FROM ecommerce.staging.orders_updates
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

steps.prompt: order_id 1001 appears twice (two CDC events). What do you need to decide which wins?

options.text: A deterministic ordering field such as event_sequence, updated_at or version
options.fb: That's what makes the pick reproducible.

options.text: Pick whichever Spark returns first
options.fb: Non-deterministic — results may change on retry.

options.text: Average the two amounts
options.fb: Invents data that never existed.

options.text: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_sequence DESC), keep rn = 1, then MERGE
options.fb: Dedup, then merge the clean source.

options.text: Add WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE
options.fb: Unrelated, and dangerous for an incremental source.

options.text: Switch to append mode
options.fb: Creates duplicates in the target instead.

exercises.explain: Find duplicates → find ordering field → dedup → merge.

exercises.q: Source has `id=10 version=1 amount=100` and `id=10 version=2 amount=120`. Before MERGE you…
options: Rank by business key ordered by `version DESC` and keep rn = 1 (amount 120)
exercises.explain: Deduplicate by business key with a deterministic ordering field. The newest version (2, amount 120) represents the latest state.

exercises.q: Write the query that finds duplicated `order_id`s in `ecommerce.staging.orders_updates`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*)
FROM ecommerce.staging.orders_updates
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
exercises.explain: The first query in the 'merge fails' workflow. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation — WHERE can't reference COUNT(*).

exercises.q: Order the phases of optimistic concurrency control.
exercises.explain: Databricks describes exactly read → write → validate-and-commit. Validation happens at the end, which is what makes it 'optimistic'.

exercises.q: Delta locks the entire table pessimistically so that concurrent writers wait for each other.
exercises.explain: Delta uses optimistic concurrency: writers work in parallel on a snapshot and conflicts are checked at commit time.

exercises.q: Why is it called **optimistic** concurrency control?
options: It assumes most concurrent transactions won't conflict and checks only at validation/commit
It optimistically skips validation for small writes
exercises.explain: It bets on 'no conflict', lets everyone work, then validates. If the bet fails, one transaction fails — the table stays consistent.

exercises.q: Table at v50. A and B both read v50. A commits v51. B's changes don't conflict with A's. What happens to B?
options: B fails because it read an old version
B validates v50→v51, finds no conflict and commits v52
exercises.explain: Reading an older version isn't itself a failure: B checks what changed since its snapshot. No conflict → it commits as the next version, v52.

exercises.q: Order the life of a MERGE as you should picture it.
exercises.explain: This is the 'data engineer' level view of MERGE: matching, file-level changes, validation, atomic commit. Seeing only 'update/insert' hides where failures and costs come from.

exercises.q: Explain optimistic concurrency control in Delta in your own words.
exercises.model: Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot of the table and prepares its new files without locking the whole table. At commit time Delta checks which commits happened since that snapshot and whether they conflict with what this transaction read or changed. If it's safe, the commit becomes a new atomic version; if not, the transaction fails (and can retry on fresh state) instead of corrupting the table.
rubric: Works on a snapshot, no pessimistic table lock
Validation at commit against concurrent commits
exercises.explain: Hit the four phases and the 'fail instead of corrupt' guarantee.

exercises.q: Table at v50. Jobs A, B, C all read v50. A commits first. B validates — no conflict — and commits. C validates — conflicts with A — and fails. What is the latest table version?
exercises.explain: A → v51, B → v52, C fails and creates no version. Failed transactions never produce versions.

exercises.q: What is the default isolation level for Delta writes on Databricks?
why: Snapshot isolation describes reads, not the write level.
exercises.explain: Default writes: **WriteSerializable**. Reads use snapshot isolation. Serializable is the stronger, opt-in level.

exercises.q: If jobs A and B change **different rows** of the **same** Parquet file, they must conflict.
exercises.explain: Not anymore: with deletion vectors and row-level concurrency they can coexist, as long as they don't change the same row and the requirements are met.

exercises.q: A: `UPDATE customers SET status='A' WHERE id=10`; B concurrently: `… status='B' WHERE id=10`. What do you expect?
options: Both succeed; last writer wins silently
A real write conflict: one commits, the other fails or is serialized safely
exercises.explain: Same-row modifications still conflict even with row-level concurrency. Optimistic validation guarantees one wins and the other fails — never inconsistent state.

exercises.q: Set the isolation level of `my_table` to Serializable.
exercises.explain: Isolation level is a table property. Serializable is stricter (reads + writes explainable by a serial order) and may cause more conflicts.

exercises.q: Match the concurrency concept.
pairs: Can coexist with DVs + row-level concurrency
exercises.explain: The memorization trio plus the row-level concurrency rule.

exercises.q: Which conditions enable row-level concurrency on Databricks? (choose all)
exercises.explain: Row-level concurrency relies on DVs and works for unpartitioned tables on supported runtimes; liquid-clustered tables also use this architecture. Isolation level and ZORDER are not prerequisites.

exercises.q: Which one does NOT belong to Delta's isolation vocabulary on Databricks?
exercises.explain: Delta writes use WriteSerializable (default) or Serializable; reads use snapshot isolation. Delta never exposes uncommitted data — that's the whole point of atomic commits.

exercises.q: Your write fails with `ConcurrentAppendException`. What does this usually mean?
options: The optimistic concurrency system prevented an unsafe commit because another operation added files your operation depended on
exercises.explain: Concurrency exceptions signal protection, not corruption. Investigate the competing writer; retry after re-reading fresh state if the conflict is transient.

exercises.q: Match each exception to its likely cause.
pairs: Another writer added files in the data you read
Another writer deleted/rewrote a file you read
Two writers share one transaction identity (e.g. stream checkpoint)
exercises.explain: Learn the cause behind each name: it tells you which *other* operation to look for in DESCRIBE HISTORY.

exercises.q: Your daily `MERGE INTO prod.silver.orders … ON t.id = s.id` fails with `DELTA_CONCURRENT_WRITE`.

options.text: Find what other writer touched the table at the same time (DESCRIBE HISTORY)
options.fb: Identify the competing transaction first.

options.text: Wrap it in a loop: run again until it works
options.fb: Hides the cause; may hammer the table and never converge.

options.text: Drop and recreate the table
options.fb: Destroys data/history; the table isn't corrupted.

steps.prompt: History shows a backfill job running MERGE on the same table. Both MERGEs scan the whole table. What helps?

options.text: Narrow the MERGE condition if semantically correct, e.g. AND t.event_date = DATE'2026-09-16'
options.fb: Smaller read scope = smaller scan and smaller conflict domain.

options.text: Switch both to INSERT OVERWRITE
options.fb: Changes semantics and still conflicts.

options.text: Lower the cluster size
options.fb: Concurrency conflicts aren't a compute problem.

options.text: Whether DVs/row-level concurrency are enabled, whether a schema ALTER runs concurrently, and add retry-after-fresh-read for transient conflicts
options.fb: Covers the remaining causes and a safe retry policy.

options.text: Set VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS
options.fb: Unrelated and dangerous.

options.text: Disable the transaction log
options.fb: Impossible and nonsensical.

exercises.explain: Concurrency debugging = who else wrote, what did both read, can scope be narrowed, schema changes?, DV/RLC available?, then retry policy.

exercises.q: Order the concurrency debugging questions (playbook order).
items: What other writer touched this table?
What rows/files/partitions did both operations read?
Are predicates too broad / can I narrow the MERGE condition?
Is a schema ALTER happening concurrently?
Are deletion vectors / row-level concurrency available?
Should the application retry after re-reading fresh state?
exercises.explain: From cause (who/what) to scope (predicates) to special causes (schema) to platform features (DV/RLC) and finally the retry policy. Retrying first is the 'bad response'.

exercises.q: Rewrite the MERGE so its ON condition is bounded to `event_date = DATE'2026-09-16'` (target `prod.silver.orders` t, source `daily_updates` s, key `id`, use `SET *`/`INSERT *`).
exercises.solution:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.orders t
USING daily_updates s
ON t.id = s.id
   AND t.event_date = DATE'2026-09-16'
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
exercises.explain: The extra bound reduces both the scan and the conflict domain — valid only if matching target rows really live on that date, otherwise rows from other dates would be inserted as duplicates.

exercises.q: The right response to a concurrency exception is to re-run the job until it succeeds.
exercises.explain: That's the 'bad response'. First understand who else wrote and why the scopes overlap. Retry logic is fine for legitimate transient conflicts — after re-reading fresh state.

exercises.q: `MetadataChangedException` during a write. What probably happened?
options: A concurrent operation changed the table metadata, e.g. ALTER TABLE or a schema-evolving write
Your SELECT used the wrong version
exercises.explain: Schema changes are metadata changes and conflict with concurrent writes (they can also stop streams reading the table until restart). Coordinate schema updates.

exercises.q: Will these two concurrent operations necessarily conflict (assume DVs + row-level concurrency enabled, unpartitioned table)?

items.text: A updates row 1, B updates row 9000 of the same file
A runs ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS while B writes
A deletes a file that B's MERGE read

exercises.explain: Same-row changes, metadata changes and deletes of files you read are real conflicts. Different rows (with RLC) and blind appends usually coexist.

exercises.q: What is `MERGE`?
options: A command that combines two tables into a new table
An atomic source-to-target operation that can update, insert and delete target rows based on matching conditions
A way to merge small files
why: It changes an existing target, it doesn't build a new table.
exercises.explain: MERGE matches source rows to target rows with an ON condition and applies UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE per case, all in one transaction (one new version). File compaction is OPTIMIZE; schema merging is mergeSchema.

exercises.q: Checkpoint V2 is a newer checkpoint design aimed at better scalability and concurrency for large or frequently updated tables.
exercises.explain: Checkpoints summarize log state in Parquet-based structures; V2 improves how that works at scale. You still shouldn't depend on when checkpoints are written.

exercises.q: Besides SQL MERGE and `DeltaTable.merge`, modern PySpark/Databricks also has a DataFrame `mergeInto()` API — all implement the same source-target matching model.
exercises.explain: Different APIs, same semantics: ON condition + matched / not matched / not matched by source clauses. Learn SQL MERGE and DeltaTable first — they dominate existing production code.

exercises.q: Complete the Python MERGE.
exercises.text:
from delta.tables import [[DeltaTable]]

target = DeltaTable.[[forName]](spark, "prod.silver.customers")
(target.alias("t")
   .[[merge]](source.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
   .[[whenMatchedUpdate]](set={"name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
   .[[whenNotMatchedInsert]](values={"id": "s.id", "name": "s.name", "city": "s.city"})
   .[[execute]]())
exercises.explain: forName loads the table by catalog name; merge(source, condition) starts the builder; whenMatchedUpdate/whenNotMatchedInsert mirror WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED; execute() runs it.

exercises.q: The source `staging.customer_changes_today` holds only today's changed customers. Which line will cause data loss?
lines: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;
exercises.fix:
MERGE INTO prod.silver.customers t
USING staging.customer_changes_today s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
exercises.explain: With an incremental source, every customer not changed today is 'not matched by source' and gets deleted. Only use that clause when the source is a full authoritative snapshot.

exercises.q: A colleague's 'mental model' notes for an UPDATE of row 2 in file A (rows 1–3). Which line is wrong?
lines: 2. Open A.parquet and overwrite row 2's bytes in place
3. Commit to _delta_log as a new version
4. Old snapshots still see the old row 2
exercises.fix: 2. Write a new file B (rows 1, 3 unchanged + new row 2) — or a DV + supplemental file — then commit REMOVE A + ADD B
exercises.explain: Parquet files are immutable. Delta writes new data (copy-on-write rewrite or deletion vector + supplemental file) and swaps it in atomically; that's also why old snapshots still work.

exercises.q: Optimistic concurrency in one sentence.
exercises.text: Each writer [[reads]] a consistent snapshot, [[writes]] candidate files without locking, then [[validates]] against commits made since its snapshot and either [[commits]] a new atomic version or fails.
exercises.explain: READ → WRITE → VALIDATE → COMMIT. Conflicts are detected at the end, not prevented with locks up front.

exercises.q: `VERSION AS OF 80` worked yesterday and fails today. Order your investigation.
items: Run DESCRIBE HISTORY on the table
Check whether a VACUUM ran and with which retention
Check whether v80's data files still exist (not just its history entry)
Conclude: time travel isn't a backup — rely on a real backup for older states
exercises.explain: History first, then the VACUUM and its retention, then the physical files. A history entry alone never proves a version is still queryable.

options.fb: Exactly the documented danger.

options.text: A concurrency conflict deleted rows
options.fb: Conflicts fail transactions, they don't delete rows.

options.text: VACUUM removed the rows
options.fb: VACUUM never changes the current snapshot.

options.text: RESTORE to the pre-MERGE version, then remove the clause (keep it only for full snapshots)

options.text: Re-run the MERGE twice
options.fb: Same result again.

options.text: Switch the source to INSERT OVERWRITE
options.fb: Another way to lose data.

exercises.explain: NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE is only safe with a full authoritative snapshot as source.
